screens.title: Basic Enemy AI and Pathfinding
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson you will learn how simple, reliable enemy behaviors are constructed. We begin by thinking of an enemy as a small state machine that can patrol between waypoints and switch to chasing when the player appears in sight. You will see why patrolling is useful for predictable triggers, why state machines keep behavior manageable, and how line-of-sight using raycasts helps avoid false detections when obstacles block view. We also cover baking a navigation mesh and using a NavMeshAgent so your enemies can navigate around geometry automatically. A concrete example you will build in the lab is a capsule enemy that moves between two waypoints and chases the player when a raycast confirms a clear line of sight. Common mistakes are easy to fix: forgetting to bake the NavMesh or moving the agent with transform updates instead of letting the NavMeshAgent handle movement. By the end you will understand the core building blocks that let you extend an enemy with search, attack, or flee behaviors. Consider: how would you change the sight range or add an attack state when the player gets very close?

screens.title: Why simple AI matters
screens.narratorSegment: Simple AI is the backbone of predictable and fun enemy interactions. At its core, AI here is not about human-level thinking but about rules that make characters act in believable ways. For example, a patrol behavior gives an enemy a routine the player can learn and exploit; predictable routes create tension because the player times their move. A chase behavior adds reactive challenge when the player is spotted. The practical advantage of simple AI is reliability: deterministic rules and explicit state transitions are easy to debug and extend. A common misconception is thinking AI must be complex to be effective — in many games, simple state-driven behaviors produce satisfying encounters when combined with good level design. As you implement these behaviors, aim for clarity: define the expected result for each state, write concise methods for each behavior, and test transitions. An example: a capsule enemy that walks between two waypoints and switches to chasing when a raycast confirms the player is visible. The takeaway is that small, well-tested rules produce gameplay that feels intelligent without complicated algorithms. Why simple AI matters means simple, well-structured behaviors deliver reliable, tunable enemy interactions that players can learn and react to.. In practical terms, how basic behaviors make a game feel alive. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Core Concept
Why simple AI matters
Small rules produce predictable, extensible behaviors that are easier to test and tune than large, opaque systems.
Concrete example
A capsule enemy patrols two waypoints. When the player is seen, it switches to chase; when lost, it returns to patrol.
Common misconception
More complexity does not always equal better gameplay. Start simple and add states only when they change player experience.
Key Takeaway

Simple state-based rules create predictable, testable enemy behavior that you can iterate on quickly.

Analogy
Think of the enemy as a guard following a shift schedule: routine until they spot something suspicious, then react. The schedule is the state machine.
Try this
Place waypoints and run the game. Change a state's speed value and observe how feel changes. This is the fastest path to learning.
Why it matters
Predictability lets players learn and outplay AI, creating emergent gameplay.
Watch out
Over-tuning speeds or angular speed can make motion look unnatural.

screens.title: State Machines for Enemy Behavior
screens.narratorSegment: A state machine models an agent by labeling mutually exclusive behaviors as states and defining transitions based on conditions. Practically, in Unity you use an enum such as EnemyState { Patrol, Chase } and store a currentState variable. In Update you branch on currentState, calling Patrol or Chase methods. This structure keeps code readable: each method handles its own responsibilities, and transitions are explicit. A concrete example is switching from Patrol to Chase when CheckForPlayerInSight returns true; the Patrol method detects this and sets currentState to Chase while also updating the NavMeshAgent speed for a more aggressive pursuit. A common misconception is mixing too many responsibilities in Update and scattering checks; instead centralize transition logic so state behaviors focus on movement and actions. Another practical tip: when leaving Chase to resume Patrol, decide whether to return immediately to the nearest waypoint or go to the last known player position — that choice shapes player experience. The takeaway: state machines make behavior predictable and easier to extend with states like Search or Attack. State Machines for Enemy Behavior means use an enum and a currentstate variable so transitions are explicit and each behavior method remains focused.. In practical terms, enums, currentstate, and clean transitions. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: Use an enum and a currentState variable so transitions are explicit and each behavior method remains focused.

content.html:
Definition
State Machines
Define explicit states and transitions so an enemy's logic is easy to follow and modify.
Minimal pattern
Use an enum, a currentState variable, and separate methods for each state's behavior. Example states: Patrol, Chase, Attack, Flee.
Misconception
Putting many unrelated checks in Update makes behavior hard to reason about. Keep transitions centralized and behaviors concise.
Example flow
Patrol runs until CheckForPlayerInSight returns true. Then set currentState to Chase and raise agent speed. While chasing, if sight is lost, set state back to Patrol.
Quick checklist
  • Define enum with all states you'll use.
  • Keep state methods single-purpose.
  • Use clear transition conditions and logs for debugging.
Key Takeaway

Explicit states and focused methods help you tune and extend enemy behavior safely.

screens.title: Implementing Patrol Behavior
screens.narratorSegment: Patrolling is one of the simplest and most useful behaviors. The idea is to provide the enemy with an array of waypoint Transforms and move toward the current waypoint until the agent reaches it, then advance to the next index. In Unity, when using NavMeshAgent it is efficient to call SetDestination on the agent with the waypoint's position. If you prefer a manual method, Vector3. MoveTowards also works for flat surfaces, but it bypasses NavMesh pathfinding and will not avoid obstacles. A robust patrol loop checks if agent. pathPending is false and agent. remainingDistance is below a small threshold before switching indices; this prevents rapid flipping when the path is still being calculated. Concrete example: two waypoints named Waypoint1 and Waypoint2 wired into the patrolPoints array; when remainingDistance < 0.5, increment currentPatrolIndex modulo the array length and call SetDestination for the new point. Misconception: setting transform. position directly on a NavMeshAgent collides with the agent's internal movement; always use SetDestination when the agent is present. The key is to keep the patrol logic deterministic so debugging transitions to chase becomes straightforward.

keyIdea.title: Patrol pattern
keyIdea.text: Use an array of waypoints and SetDestination to cycle smoothly; check remainingDistance before switching to the next point.

content.html:
Process Flow
Patrol: waypoints → destination
Cycle an index through patrolPoints and set the agent destination each time a point is reached.
1
Set initial destination
In Start, if patrolPoints length > 0 set agent.SetDestination(patrolPoints[0].position).
2
Check arrival
If !agent.pathPending and agent.remainingDistance < threshold, advance the index and SetDestination to next point.
3
Loop
Use modulo arithmetic so patrol repeats: currentPatrolIndex = (currentPatrolIndex + 1) % patrolPoints.Length.
Concrete scenario
Two empty GameObjects named Waypoint1 and Waypoint2 placed in the scene form a simple patrol. Assign them to the script array and watch the enemy cycle.
Pro-tip
Use small thresholds like 0.5 for remainingDistance to avoid premature switching while the agent is still computing the path.
Key Takeaway

Patrol with SetDestination and check remainingDistance; never move a NavMeshAgent by changing transform.position.

screens.title: Implementing Chase Behavior
screens.narratorSegment: Chase behavior continuously updates the enemy's destination to the player's current position so the NavMeshAgent finds a path as the player moves. The simplest implementation calls agent. SetDestination(player. position) each frame while in the Chase state. Increase the agent's speed to make the pursuit feel urgent, but be careful not to set angularSpeed or acceleration so high that movement looks jittery. A practical example: when your CheckForPlayerInSight returns true, switch currentState to Chase, set agent. speed to chaseSpeed, and in ChaseBehavior update SetDestination with playerTarget. position. When the player is lost, decide whether to resume patrol immediately or move to the last known player position. A common pitfall is checking distance only — the agent may attempt to move through obstacles to reach the player. Raycasting addresses this by confirming a clear line of sight before the transition. The learning goal is to make chase responsive without sacrificing believable motion by tuning agent parameters and transition rules. keyIdea.title: Chase pattern
keyIdea.text: While in Chase state, update the NavMeshAgent destination to the player's current position and tune speeds for believable pursuit.

content.html:
Process Flow
Chase: follow the player
Continuously set the agent destination to the player's transform so the agent recalculates a path as the player moves.
Behavior
In Chase, call agent.SetDestination(playerTarget.position) each Update while the player remains in sight.
Tuning tips
  • chaseSpeed > patrolSpeed for clear urgency.
  • Keep angularSpeed reasonable to avoid snapping turns.
  • Use acceleration to smooth starts and stops.
Concrete example
When transitioning to Chase, agent.speed = chaseSpeed; while chasing, agent.SetDestination(playerTarget.position); if sight is lost, return to Patrol and reset speed.
Common mistake
Using only Vector3.Distance to trigger chase can cause enemies to try to walk through obstacles. Add a raycast to check visibility.
Key Takeaway

Keep chase responsive by updating destination each frame and tune agent parameters to preserve believable motion.

screens.title: Distance Check vs Raycasting
screens.narratorSegment: Distance checks are the simplest form of detection: compute the distance between enemy and player and compare it to a sightRange threshold. This is cheap and works well in open, obstacle-free spaces. However, distance alone produces false positives when the player is behind walls. Raycasting improves detection by firing an invisible ray toward the player and checking whether the ray hits an obstacle layer before the player; if the ray reaches the player collider, line of sight is clear. In practice, combine both: first check distance to avoid unnecessary raycasts beyond sightRange, then raycast only if the player is within that range. A concrete implementation pattern is: if Vector3. Distance < sightRange then compute directionToPlayer and Physics. Raycast from enemy position plus a small upward offset; if the raycast hits the player collider, the player is visible. A common misconception is that raycasts always fix detection; they must be configured with correct layers and origin offsets to avoid hitting the ground or small obstacles. The practical lesson: use distance to filter and raycast to confirm. Distance Check vs Raycasting means use a cheap distance filter, then raycast to confirm a clear line of sight before switching to chase.. In practical terms, when to use distance alone and when to verify line of sight. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: Use a cheap distance filter, then raycast to confirm a clear line of sight before switching to Chase.

content.html:
Comparison
Distance vs Raycast
Combine a distance filter with a raycast to balance performance and accuracy.
Distance Check
Cheap and broad; use Vector3.Distance to quickly reject far-away players.
Raycast
Expensive but precise; cast a ray and check obstacleLayer to confirm visibility.
Practical pattern
First check distance < sightRange. If true, compute directionToPlayer and raycast from slightly above the enemy to avoid ground collision. If the ray hits the player, set state to Chase.
Misconfiguration
If obstacleLayer is set incorrectly, raycasts may ignore obstacles or hit unwanted layers. Double-check layer masks.
Key Takeaway

Filter by distance, then raycast to confirm. Correct layer masks and origin offsets are essential.

screens.title: Raycasting and CheckForPlayerInSight
screens.narratorSegment: Let's examine the key sight-checking method that moves an enemy from Patrol to Chase. The method begins with a distance test: if the player is further than sightRange, return false immediately. If the player is within range, compute the normalized direction and perform a Physics. Raycast from the enemy's position plus a small upward offset to avoid hitting the ground. Provide an obstacleLayer to the raycast so only environment geometry is considered. When the raycast stores its hit, check whether the collider carries the Player tag; if so, we have line of sight. This sequence avoids unnecessary raycasts beyond sightRange and reliably handles obstacles. A common mistake is performing the raycast without any upward offset, which can hit the floor or small objects and give false negatives. Another is using an incorrect layer mask that inadvertently filters out the environment. The concrete example in the provided EnemyAI script uses this exact pattern, and visualizing rays with OnDrawGizmos helps debug sight during play. Try blocking the ray to confirm behavior changes. Raycasting and CheckForPlayerInSight means distance filter → raycast from slight height → check hit collider tag to confirm player visibility.. keyIdea.title: Sight check
keyIdea.text: Distance filter → raycast from slight height → check hit collider tag to confirm player visibility.

content.html:
Code Walkthrough
CheckForPlayerInSight method
// Distance filter first
float distanceToPlayer = Vector3.Distance(transform.position, playerTarget.position);
if (distanceToPlayer < sightRange)
{
  Vector3 directionToPlayer = (playerTarget.position - transform.position).normalized;
  RaycastHit hit;
  // Raycast from slightly above to avoid immediate ground hits
  if (Physics.Raycast(transform.position + Vector3.up * 0.5f, directionToPlayer, out hit, sightRange, obstacleLayer))
  {
    if (hit.collider.CompareTag("Player"))
    {
      return true; // Player visible
    }
  }
}
return false; // Not visible
Explanation
  • Distance check reduces raycast calls for performance.
  • Raycast uses an obstacle layer mask to ignore non-environment colliders.
  • An upward offset prevents hitting the ground immediately.
  • Compare the hit collider tag to detect the player specifically.
Debug tip

Use OnDrawGizmos or Debug.DrawRay to visualize the ray in the editor and confirm origin and direction.

screens.title: NavMesh: Bake Walkable Surfaces
screens.narratorSegment: NavMesh baking converts scene geometry into a data structure that agents use to find paths. The steps are straightforward: mark ground and static obstacles as Navigation Static in the Inspector, open the Navigation window, and click Bake to generate the blue walkable overlay. This overlay is what NavMeshAgent consults when computing paths. void Start()
{
  agent = GetComponent<NavMeshAgent>();

  {

void PatrolBehavior(bool playerInSight)
{
  if (!agent.pathPending && agent.remainingDistance < 0.5f)
  {

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson you will learn how simple, reliable enemy behaviors are constructed. We begin by thinking of an enemy as a small state machine that can patrol between waypoints and switch to chasing when the player appears in sight. You will see why patrolling is useful for predictable triggers, why state machines keep behavior manageable, and how line-of-sight using raycasts helps avoid false detections when obstacles block view. We also cover baking a navigation mesh and using a NavMeshAgent so your enemies can navigate around geometry automatically. A concrete example you will build in the lab is a capsule enemy that moves between two waypoints and chases the player when a raycast confirms a clear line of sight. Common mistakes are easy to fix: forgetting to bake the NavMesh or moving the agent with transform updates instead of letting the NavMeshAgent handle movement. By the end you will understand the core building blocks that let you extend an enemy with search, attack, or flee behaviors. Consider: how would you change the sight range or add an attack state when the player gets very close?

These objectives focus your attention on the practical skills you'll build. First, you'll design simple AI behaviors like patrolling and chasing so non-player characters feel purposeful rather than random. An example is creating patrol waypoints so an enemy moves predictably until it sees the player. Second, you'll implement a basic state machine to manage behavior transitions; using an enum for states makes logic readable and maintainable. Third, you will use Unity's NavMesh system to let agents compute paths around obstacles instead of manually steering them, which reduces bugs and improves realism. Fourth, you will apply raycasting for line-of-sight detection so the enemy only chases when the player is truly visible. Each objective maps to a hands-on step in the lab: bake a NavMesh, configure a NavMeshAgent, add waypoints, and write a CheckForPlayerInSight method. As you practice, frequently test a misconception: distance alone is not sufficient for sight — raycasting matters when obstacles are present. These core skills let you extend the AI later with search, attack, or fleeing states.

This second objectives screen emphasizes practice checks and small extensions you can add after completing the lab. For patrolling and chasing, verify behavior by placing the player near waypoints and observing that the enemy resumes patrol when the player leaves sight. For the state machine, test each transition explicitly and log state names when they change to ensure your logic is clear. For NavMesh, validate by intentionally adding an un-baked surface and observing that the agent fails to move; this exposes the common baking mistake. For raycasting, test by putting an obstacle between the enemy and player so the distance check would pass but the raycast blocks the chase. Each practice test builds confidence and reveals common pitfalls. Once you're comfortable, try adding a brief Search or Attack state as a variation. These small experiments teach how tiny changes to conditions or agent settings alter emergent gameplay, and they let you iterate quickly when tuning difficulty or responsiveness.

Simple AI is the backbone of predictable and fun enemy interactions. At its core, AI here is not about human-level thinking but about rules that make characters act in believable ways. For example, a patrol behavior gives an enemy a routine the player can learn and exploit; predictable routes create tension because the player times their move. A chase behavior adds reactive challenge when the player is spotted. The practical advantage of simple AI is reliability: deterministic rules and explicit state transitions are easy to debug and extend. A common misconception is thinking AI must be complex to be effective — in many games, simple state-driven behaviors produce satisfying encounters when combined with good level design. As you implement these behaviors, aim for clarity: define the expected result for each state, write concise methods for each behavior, and test transitions. An example: a capsule enemy that walks between two waypoints and switches to chasing when a raycast confirms the player is visible. The takeaway is that small, well-tested rules produce gameplay that feels intelligent without complicated algorithms. A state machine models an agent by labeling mutually exclusive behaviors as states and defining transitions based on conditions. Practically, in Unity you use an enum such as EnemyState { Patrol, Chase } and store a currentState variable. In Update you branch on currentState, calling Patrol or Chase methods. This structure keeps code readable: each method handles its own responsibilities, and transitions are explicit. A concrete example is switching from Patrol to Chase when CheckForPlayerInSight returns true; the Patrol method detects this and sets currentState to Chase while also updating the NavMeshAgent speed for a more aggressive pursuit. A common misconception is mixing too many responsibilities in Update and scattering checks; instead centralize transition logic so state behaviors focus on movement and actions. Another practical tip: when leaving Chase to resume Patrol, decide whether to return immediately to the nearest waypoint or go to the last known player position — that choice shapes player experience. Patrolling is one of the simplest and most useful behaviors. The idea is to provide the enemy with an array of waypoint Transforms and move toward the current waypoint until the agent reaches it, then advance to the next index. In Unity, when using NavMeshAgent it is efficient to call SetDestination on the agent with the waypoint's position. If you prefer a manual method, Vector3. MoveTowards also works for flat surfaces, but it bypasses NavMesh pathfinding and will not avoid obstacles. A robust patrol loop checks if agent. pathPending is false and agent. remainingDistance is below a small threshold before switching indices; this prevents rapid flipping when the path is still being calculated. Chase behavior continuously updates the enemy's destination to the player's current position so the NavMeshAgent finds a path as the player moves. The simplest implementation calls agent.
